lesson.title: Negative Exponents: Flipping to the Other Side
lesson.summary: A negative exponent is not a negative number in disguise; it is an instruction to take the reciprocal, a direct consequence of the same product rule that governs every integer exponent.
lesson.body:
A negative exponent tells you to take the reciprocal of the base raised to the corresponding positive exponent: a^(-n) = 1/(a^n), for any nonzero base a. For example, 2^(-3) = 1/(2^3) = 1/8. A negative exponent never makes the result negative; it only flips the expression into a fraction. This can surprise students who expect a negative sign anywhere to produce a negative number, but exponents behave differently from ordinary multiplication signs.

This definition is not an arbitrary rule to memorize; it falls directly out of the product rule for integer exponents. Consider a^3 * a^(-3). By the product rule, this equals a^(3 + (-3)) = a^0 = 1. But a^3 * a^(-3) equaling 1 means a^(-3) must be the multiplicative inverse of a^3, which is exactly 1/(a^3). So negative exponents are really just the inverse property, covered at the very start of this unit, applied to powers instead of plain numbers.

Negative exponents also appear in the denominator and flip upward as positive ones. Since a^(-n) = 1/(a^n), it follows that 1/(a^(-n)) = a^n, because flipping a fraction twice returns the original. This means an expression like x^(-2) in a denominator, such as 1/(x^(-2)), simplifies to x^2. A useful shortcut: moving a factor across the fraction bar, from numerator to denominator or denominator to numerator, always flips the sign of its exponent.

Worked example: simplify (3^(-2) * 3^5) / 3^(-1). First combine the numerator using the product rule: 3^(-2) * 3^5 = 3^(-2+5) = 3^3. Then apply the quotient rule: 3^3 / 3^(-1) = 3^(3-(-1)) = 3^4 = 81. Check by computing each piece numerically: 3^(-2) = 1/9, 3^5 = 243, so the numerator is (1/9)(243) = 27. The denominator is 3^(-1) = 1/3. Dividing, 27 / (1/3) = 27 * 3 = 81, which matches the exponent rule answer exactly.

A common mistake is applying the negative sign to the base instead of taking the reciprocal: 2^(-3) is not -8 and not -2^3; it equals 1/8. Keeping the base and exponent rules separate from ordinary sign rules for multiplication avoids this error. Another useful pattern: a negative exponent on a fraction flips the entire fraction and drops the negative sign, so (2/3)^(-2) = (3/2)^2 = 9/4, since flipping 2/3 to its reciprocal 3/2 and then squaring gives the same result as first squaring 2/3 to get 4/9 and then taking the reciprocal, which is also 9/4.

Negative exponents build on integer exponents, extending the same product and quotient rules to exponents below zero without breaking them. They also combine naturally with rational exponents from the previous section: an expression like 16^(-1/2) means take the reciprocal of 16^(1/2), so 16^(-1/2) = 1/(16^(1/2)) = 1/4, since the square root of 16 is 4. With integer, rational, and now negative exponents all governed by the same three core rules, product, quotient, and power of a power, you have a complete, unified system for handling any exponent that appears in algebra.
